stops.name: Venice, victory, and the word 'mutilated'
stops.campa: As the last offensive opens on the Piave, he publishes in the Corriere della Sera the letter to the dead: our Victory, you shall not be mutilated. The phrase outlives the war it was written to bless. When the armistice comes and the diplomats at Paris begin trimming the Adriatic promises, vittoria mutilata is already minted, waiting in every mouth. The poet has done the most dangerous of his deeds: he has given a grievance its name. Names, in his hands, mobilize like divisions.

stops.name: Ronchi, the night muster of the granatieri
stops.campa: In the night of 11-12 September 1919, at Ronchi where the grenadiers expelled from Fiume wait in their billets, the Comandante arrives by motorcar, feverish, to lead the march the government has forbidden. Some two hundred men and a column of commandeered trucks: the marcia di Ronchi. He tells them the die is cast and better than Caesar's, for they cross not a river but a sentence of the diplomats. The village will take the name Ronchi dei Legionari from this night, the calendar of the myth beginning at its gate.

stops.name: Cantrida, the roadblock, the breast of medals
stops.campa: At Cantrida, on the western approach to Fiume, General Pittaluga's armoured cars bar the road with orders to stop the column at any cost. The Comandante descends, opens his greatcoat over the gold medal and the ribbons of the war, and offers the general his chest: fire on these first. The soldiers sent to stop him present arms instead; the armoured cars swing round and join the column. The canon records the moment as the modern miracle of the loaves: an army fed to the rebellion by the act of refusing to shoot it.
stops.quote_source: To General Pittaluga at Cantrida, 12 September 1919 (as recorded in the Fiume chronicles and Pittaluga's memoirs)

stops.name: Fiume, the Santa Entrata
stops.campa: Toward noon of 12 September 1919 the column enters Fiume through streets gone mad with flowers and flags sewn in secret. Women weep on the running-boards; the bells of the Italian churches ring themselves hoarse. The city that the Peace Conference has assigned to no one receives its Comandante as a bridegroom: the tradition names the day the Santa Entrata, the Holy Entry, and means the Gospel echo. A poet has taken a city with two hundred men and a fever, and not one shot has been required of history.

stops.name: Fiume, the balcony of the Governor's Palace, the proclamation
stops.campa: At six in the evening, still burning with fever, he steps onto the balcony of the Governor's Palace above a piazza packed to the walls. In the mad and vile world, he tells them, Fiume is today the sign of liberty; there is one truth, and it is Fiume; one love, and it is Fiume. He proclaims the annexation to Italy in the name of the sound people of the nation and asks the crowd to confirm its vote before the flag of the Timavo: the Randaccio banner spread on the parapet. The piazza thunders yes three times. The Comandante governs from this balcony for fifteen months.
stops.quote: Italiani di Fiume! Nel mondo folle e vile, Fiume oggi è il segno della libertà; nel mondo folle e vile vi è una sola cosa pura: Fiume; vi è una sola verità: e questa è Fiume; vi è un solo amore: e questo è Fiume!
stops.quote_source: Proclamation from the Governor's Palace balcony, 12 September 1919

stops.name: Fiume, the modus vivendi refused, Hic manebimus optime
stops.campa: In December Rome offers the compromise: the modus vivendi, an Italian protectorate in ordinary prose. The city's council inclines to accept; the plebiscite of 18 December votes for it; and the Comandante, reading in the urns a will unworthy of the dead, annuls the count and answers with the old Roman word: here we shall remain, excellently. Fiume passes from adventure to heresy: a city-state run on orations, piracy and festival, where deserters arrive weekly and the futurists, the syndicalists and the uscocchi of the new age gather as at a court of miracles.
stops.quote_source: Motto adopted by d'Annunzio at Fiume, December 1919

stops.name: Fiume, the Carta del Carnaro, music made a fundamental institution
stops.campa: On 8 September 1920 he proclaims the Reggenza Italiana del Carnaro and gives it the constitution drafted with Alceste De Ambris and rewritten in his own tongue: the Carta del Carnaro. Corporations and communes, equality of women, freedom of every cult; and, alone among the constitutions of the earth, music enthroned as a religious and social institution of the state, with choirs and instruments decreed for every commune and an auditorium of ten thousand souls. The lawgiver-poet completes the arc begun at Quarto: the state itself composed as a lyric.
stops.quote: Nella Reggenza italiana del Carnaro la Musica è una istituzione religiosa e sociale.
stops.quote_source: Carta del Carnaro, article LXIV (Della Musica), 8 September 1920

stops.name: Fiume, the Natale di sangue, the Christmas of Blood
stops.campa: The Treaty of Rapallo makes Fiume a free state and the Comandante refuses the gift as an amputation. At Christmas 1920 the regular army and navy of Italy move against the city of Italians: the Natale di sangue. On 26 December the battleship Andrea Doria puts a shell into the Governor's Palace itself, the splinters falling in the Comandante's rooms. Legionaries die under Italian guns at Italian walls. He had sworn Fiume o morte; confronting instead this fratricide, he declares that Italy is not worth the dying of her best sons, and the myth chooses survival: to build its shrine elsewhere.

stops.name: Fiume, the farewell of the Comandante
stops.campa: On 18 January 1921, the powers signed away and the dead buried, the Comandante leaves Fiume by motorcar as quietly as he entered it loudly. The city lines the streets in silence; many of the legionaries weep, and some will wander for years like soldiers of a disbanded crusade. He carries away the flag of Randaccio, the ashes of his dead, and the working model of every theatrical seizure of power the century will stage. Behind him the holocaust city, la Città olocausta, the city offered whole, enters the martyrology he wrote for it.

stops.name: Gardone Riviera, Villa Cargnacco taken above the lake
stops.campa: In February 1921 he rents, then possesses, the villa of Cargnacco on the hill over Gardone Riviera: a sequestered German scholar's house with a library and a view of the whole of Garda. The same water Goethe rowed under the cliffs of Malcesine glitters below; the lake of the northern pilgrims becomes the lake of the last condottiere. He announces a retreat and begins, immediately, a construction: not a house but a self, built in stone, to be called the Vittoriale degli Italiani: the shrine of Italian victories, of which he is the chief exhibit.

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the fall from the window, the flight of the archangel
stops.campa: On the night of 13 August 1922, on the eve of a meeting with Mussolini and Nitti that might have set him at the head of the national movement, the Comandante falls from a window of the Prioria and fractures his skull. Pushed, jumped, or slipped beside the sister of his mistress; the canon leaves the agent unnamed and calls the event il volo dell'arcangelo, the archangel's flight. He lies between death and life while the March on Rome is prepared by other men. When he wakes, the century has been assigned to Mussolini, and the poet has been assigned to the lake.

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the March on Rome passes by in silence
stops.campa: October 1922: the blackshirts march on Rome using his choreography, the oaths, the songs, the Roman salute, the balcony, all inventoried at Fiume, and the inventor keeps to his hill, convalescent and unconsulted. He neither blesses nor curses; his silence is read in Rome twice a day like a barometer. The regime will pay for that silence lavishly for sixteen years: editions of his works at state expense, the Vittoriale funded, honours heaped: the gilded muzzle. He accepts the gold and, in letters, occasionally bites.
